Mzab gundi (Massoutiera mzabi) is a small, diurnal rodent inhabiting the rocky desert landscapes of the central Sahara. Neonates of this species enter the world at a remarkably modest size, with field records indicating a birth mass of approximately 20.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 20.5 grams]. This relatively low neonatal weight is characteristic of altricial rodent young and is associated with a substantial energetic investment in gestation. The developmental trajectory from this humble beginning culminates in an ultimate adult body mass of around 195 grams [Wwi = around 195 grams], a figure that positions the Mzab gundi among the medium-sized members of the family Ctenodactylidae. This nearly tenfold increase in mass from birth to adulthood underscores a rapid period of post-natal growth that is supported by a mother’s rich, high-fat milk. The species' compact body form and low surface-area-to-volume ratio are likely adaptations for thermoregulation in an environment characterized by extreme diurnal temperature fluctuations. Comparative data from related gundis suggest that such an adult mass represents an optimal trade-off between the thermal inertia needed to buffer against cold desert nights and the agility required to evade predators like the desert monitor lizard and sand fox.

Field surveys conducted in the rocky plateaus of the Tassili n'Ajjer have provided key insights into the Mzab gundi's lifespan. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of their natural habitat, where average body temperatures are regulated near 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan is estimated at approximately 5.8 years [am = approximately 5.8 years], a value derived from longitudinal mark-recapture studies on the congeneric species Ctenodactylus gundi. This longevity is surprisingly high for a rodent of its body size and points to a relatively slow life-history pace, likely linked to the low and unpredictable food resources available in arid ecosystems. Such a life expectancy requires a robust capacity for managing oxidative stress and maintaining physiological function over several seasons of resource scarcity and intense solar radiation. The attainment of this advanced age in the wild is a testament to the species' behavioral adaptations, including its reliance on deep rock crevices for predator avoidance and thermal buffering. Comparatively, the Mzab gundi's lifespan aligns more closely with that of other long-lived, social rodents like the naked mole-rat than with typical murid rodents of equivalent mass.

Reproductive activity in the Mzab gundi is timed to coincide with the brief pulses of vegetation following sporadic rainfall. The gestation period, measured during controlled laboratory conditions at a stable core body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], lasts for 73 days [tg = 73 days], a remarkably extended duration for a rodent of this size. This lengthy gestation is on the upper end of the range for the family Ctenodactylidae, with some field reports noting a span of 69 to 79 days (69-79 days) [tg = 69-79 days] depending on local resource availability and maternal condition at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. The extended intrauterine development is consistent with the birth of relatively precocial young that are well-furred and capable of limited locomotion soon after parturition. This strategy likely reduces the vulnerability of the offspring to hypothermia in the cold desert nights and allows for a shorter period of intense maternal care. Following birth, the altricial but developed pups rely entirely on their mother's milk for sustenance. The onset of nutritional independence from milk, or weaning, occurs at 65 days after birth [tx = 65 days after birth] when the young begin to forage for dry grasses and seeds alongside the mother at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. The maternal investment in lactation, spanning 65 days since parturition [tx = 65 days since parturition], is notably longer than in many similarly-sized desert rodents, reflecting the challenges of weaning in an environment with unpredictable food resources at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C].

Females typically produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], a rate constrained by the long gestation and extended lactation period as well as the short window of resource abundance. Each litter is small, consisting of 2 to 3 pups [N_R_i = consisting of 2 to 3 pups], which minimizes the energetic burden on the mother while ensuring that each offspring receives substantial maternal investment. The onset of sexual maturity is delayed relative to many other small rodents, with individuals becoming reproductively active at 11.5 months after birth [tp = 11.5 months after birth] at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This lengthy period of juvenile development, averaging approximately 350 days from birth [tp = approximately 350 days from birth] to puberty, reflects the time required to acquire the body size and fat reserves necessary to support both the demands of a protracted gestation and the energetic costs of lactation in a harsh environment at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C].

Physiologically, the Mzab gundi is a master of water conservation and thermoregulation. Stable core body temperatures are maintained around 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C] through a combination of behavioral microhabitat selection and metabolic adjustments. This thermal set point is critical for ensuring the proper function of developmental and reproductive processes; a stable thermal environment is essential for the 73-day gestation period (73 days) [tg = 73 days] and the subsequent growth of the nursing pup at a temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. The species' reliance on a few, well-provisioned offspring, combined with its extended development and long lifespan, clearly distinguishes its life-history strategy from that of rapidly reproducing, early-maturing rodents typical of more mesic habitats. This pattern suggests that the Mzab gundi's evolutionary success in the Sahara is tied closely to the ability to buffer its internal physiology against the environmental extremes, thereby enabling the slow and steady investment in individual offspring that ultimately ensures a high rate of juvenile survival in a world of scarce, unpredictable resources.
